subtopic_detail: Eight months of abdominal pain relieved by opening the bowels with alternating stool form and a normal faecal calprotectin
stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman referred with eight months of lower abdominal cramping. She tells you the pain eases once she has opened her bowels and that her motions swing between hard pellets and loose stools from week to week, often with bloating that worsens through the day.

She has not lost weight, has never woken at night with the pain and has never seen blood. Nobody in her family has had bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. She has brought printouts about bowel cancer and wants a colonoscopy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2 with no documented weight change, abdomen soft with mild non localised tenderness and no mass, no perianal disease, no clubbing, no mouth ulcers, no abdominal distension on examination
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30 to 200), coeliac serology negative with a normal total immunoglobulin A, faecal calprotectin 26 micrograms/g (less than 50), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her for colonoscopy to exclude an organic cause before committing to any symptomatic treatment for her abdominal symptoms
options.rationale: Colonoscopy in a woman under fifty with no alarm features, normal inflammatory markers and a normal calprotectin has a diagnostic yield little different from the background population and carries procedural risk. It is indicated for rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, a family history of bowel cancer or symptom onset after fifty. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Arrange a gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies to exclude coeliac disease despite the negative serology and reassess her symptoms afterwards
options.rationale: Negative coeliac serology with a normal total immunoglobulin A makes coeliac disease very unlikely, so biopsy adds risk without meaningful yield. Biopsy despite negative serology is reserved for patients already on a gluten free diet or with immunoglobulin A deficiency. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Explain the positive diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome and refer her to a dietitian for a supervised trial of a low fermentable carbohydrate diet
options.rationale: Pain related to defaecation with a change in stool form and frequency, in the absence of alarm features and with normal screening tests, meets the criteria for irritable bowel syndrome, which is a positive diagnosis rather than one of exclusion. A dietitian supervised low fermentable carbohydrate diet improves symptoms in around three quarters of patients and includes a structured reintroduction phase. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks and review her abdominal pain and bloating in the clinic once the course is complete
options.rationale: Acid suppression does not treat pain that is relieved by defaecation and has no effect on stool form or bloating. A proton pump inhibitor trial is appropriate for epigastric burning or reflux symptoms, which she does not describe. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome

options.text: Request a faecal occult blood test and repeat it in three months to provide her with reassurance about the possibility of bowel cancer
options.rationale: Immunochemical faecal testing is a population screening tool for asymptomatic people and is not validated for investigating symptoms, so a negative result cannot be used as reassurance in a symptomatic patient. Symptomatic patients meeting referral criteria go to colonoscopy directly rather than to stool testing. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

explanation.summary: Irritable bowel syndrome affects around one in seven Australians and is diagnosed positively on recurrent abdominal pain related to defaecation or associated with a change in stool frequency or form, present for at least six months. A limited screening panel of full blood count, C-reactive protein, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin is sufficient in a young patient without alarm features, and normal results make inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease very unlikely. Alarm features that shift the approach are unintentional weight loss, rectal bleeding, iron deficiency anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, a family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease, and onset after the age of fifty. Treatment begins with explanation and dietary modification, with the low fermentable oligosaccharide, disaccharide, monosaccharide and polyol approach developed in Australia having the strongest dietary evidence, delivered with dietitian supervision because of the risk of nutritional inadequacy and disordered eating if the restriction phase is prolonged. Second line options are directed at the predominant symptom, and gut brain neuromodulators and gut directed hypnotherapy help refractory pain.
key_points: The diagnosis is positive, based on pain related to defaecation with a change in stool form or frequency.
A normal calprotectin with normal inflammatory markers makes inflammatory bowel disease very unlikely.
Alarm features include weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms and onset after fifty.
A dietitian supervised low fermentable carbohydrate diet is the dietary treatment with the best evidence.
Faecal immunochemical testing is a screening tool and is not validated for symptomatic patients.
explanation.pearls: Keep the restriction phase of a low fermentable carbohydrate diet to two to six weeks and insist on structured reintroduction, because prolonged restriction reduces beneficial colonic bacteria and calcium and fibre intake, and is a recognised trigger for disordered eating patterns.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Irritable bowel syndrome
Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines
NICE: Irritable bowel syndrome in adults

subtopic_detail: Two years of recurrent painful lumps in both armpits and the groin with rope like scarring and discharging tunnels
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 24 year old woman referred after four courses of flucloxacillin in the past year. She describes painful lumps in both armpits and her groin that swell, burst and discharge, then come back in a slightly different spot a few weeks later.

She has stopped wearing sleeveless tops and has taken sick leave because of the pain and the smell. She smokes fifteen cigarettes a day. She has no fever and feels systemically well between episodes.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, multiple tender inflammatory nodules in both axillae and both groins with several double headed open comedones, rope like scarring across the left axilla and two sinus tracts discharging on gentle pressure, no involvement of the face or trunk, no fever
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (less than 5), swab from a discharging lesion growing mixed skin flora, fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a further two week course of flucloxacillin and advise her to return promptly if the lesions recur again after treatment
options.rationale: Short antistaphylococcal courses treat the disorder as recurrent boils, which is why she has relapsed four times, and the swab growing mixed flora reflects colonisation rather than a primary infection. Flucloxacillin is the right drug for a genuine staphylococcal abscess in previously normal skin. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

options.text: Refer her directly for wide surgical excision of both axillae and both groins as the definitive treatment for her recurrent lesions
options.rationale: Wide excision has a role in burnt out fibrotic disease at Hurley stage three but is disfiguring and does not address active inflammation elsewhere. Medical therapy is offered first, with surgery reserved for localised persistent tracts once inflammation is controlled. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

options.text: Arrange incision and drainage of each fluctuant lesion under local anaesthetic and review her in the surgical clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Simple incision and drainage gives brief relief but the lesions recur at the same sites and the procedure adds to the scarring burden, so it is not a treatment for the disease. It is appropriate for acute pain relief of a tense abscess alongside, never instead of, disease modifying therapy. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

options.text: Prescribe topical mupirocin to both axillae and the groin and arrange nasal decolonisation for her and her household contacts
options.rationale: Decolonisation targets recurrent staphylococcal furunculosis, which does not produce sinus tracts, double headed comedones or the characteristic scarring seen here. It would be the right approach to genuinely recurrent boils with a consistent staphylococcal isolate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Commence oral doxycycline for at least three months with smoking cessation support and refer her to a dermatology service for ongoing care
options.rationale: Double headed comedones with sinus tracts and rope like scarring in both axillae and groins is hidradenitis suppurativa at Hurley stage two, for which a tetracycline given for three months or longer is the standard systemic first line treatment in Australian practice. Smoking is the strongest modifiable driver of severity and cessation support belongs in the initial plan rather than as an afterthought. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

explanation.summary: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a chronic inflammatory disease of the follicular unit in apocrine bearing skin, affecting around one per cent of the population with a strong female preponderance and a typical onset in the twenties. It is very commonly misdiagnosed as recurrent boils, and the average delay to correct diagnosis remains around seven years, during which patients receive repeated short antibiotic courses and incision and drainage procedures that do nothing to alter the disease. The diagnostic triad is typical lesions including nodules, abscesses, double headed comedones and sinus tracts, in typical locations of axillae, groin, inframammary and perianal skin, with a chronic relapsing course. Severity is staged by the Hurley system, with stage one being isolated nodules, stage two recurrent lesions with tracts and scarring separated by normal skin, and stage three diffuse interconnected tracts across an entire area. Smoking and obesity are the major modifiable factors, topical clindamycin suits stage one, tetracyclines are first line systemic therapy, and biologic therapy with adalimumab is available for moderate to severe disease that fails conventional treatment.
key_points: Double headed comedones and sinus tracts distinguish the disease from recurrent boils.
Typical sites are axillae, groin, inframammary and perianal skin.
Repeated short antibiotic courses and drainage procedures do not modify the disease.
Tetracyclines given for three months or longer are first line systemic therapy.
Smoking and obesity are the strongest modifiable drivers of severity.
explanation.pearls: Screen every patient with hidradenitis suppurativa for depression and for inflammatory bowel disease, since rates of suicidal ideation are around twice those of other dermatological patients and Crohn disease is several times more common than in the general population and shares the perianal phenotype.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Hidradenitis suppurativa

subtopic_detail: Isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with a warm bowed shin and progressive hearing loss in a man in his seventies
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 72 year old man referred with an abnormal blood test found when his general practitioner investigated tiredness. He mentions a dull ache in his right shin that has been present for about a year and is worse at night, and says he has needed the television louder over the past two years.

He has no history of cancer and has not lost weight. He takes no regular medications and drinks two standard drinks a week.

data_table.Examination: Anterior bowing of the right tibia with skin over it warmer than the left, no localised bony tenderness to percussion over the spine, conductive pattern hearing loss on the right with Rinne negative on that side, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, normal power and sensation in both legs
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 412 U/L (30 to 110), gamma glutamyl transferase 24 U/L (less than 60), bilirubin and transaminases within normal limits, corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 72 nmol/L (greater than 50), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60 to 110), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure serum parathyroid hormone to establish whether the bone turnover is being driven by parathyroid overactivity
options.rationale: Hyperparathyroidism raises alkaline phosphatase but does so with hypercalcaemia and a low or low normal phosphate, and his calcium, phosphate and vitamin D are all normal. Parathyroid hormone is the right test when calcium is abnormal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Request serum and urine protein electrophoresis with serum free light chains to look for a monoclonal paraprotein as the underlying cause
options.rationale: Myeloma characteristically produces a normal or low alkaline phosphatase because its lesions are purely lytic with suppressed osteoblastic activity, so a markedly raised level argues against it. Electrophoresis is warranted with anaemia, renal impairment, hypercalcaemia or unexplained bone pain with lytic lesions. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase

options.text: Request plain radiographs of the symptomatic tibia together with a whole body radionuclide bone scan to define the distribution of disease
options.rationale: An isolated rise in alkaline phosphatase with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase confirms a bony rather than hepatic source, and bowing with overlying warmth alongside hearing loss is Paget disease of bone, in which plain films characterise the lesion and a bone scan maps every affected site. Mapping the distribution matters because asymptomatic skull or vertebral involvement changes management. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to search for a primary malignancy with skeletal metastatic disease
options.rationale: Metastatic bone disease is the important differential but it would be unusual to produce a year of localised pain with bowing of a long bone and no weight loss, anaemia or known primary. Cross sectional imaging becomes appropriate if the bone scan shows a pattern inconsistent with Paget disease. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase

options.text: Commence oral alendronate weekly and recheck the alkaline phosphatase level in three months to confirm a response to treatment
options.rationale: Starting treatment before imaging leaves the diagnosis unconfirmed and the extent of disease unknown, and oral weekly bisphosphonate dosing is an osteoporosis regimen rather than the intensive dosing used in Paget disease. Treatment follows confirmation, and a single zoledronic acid infusion is the usual Australian choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

explanation.summary: Paget disease of bone is a focal disorder of excessive and disorganised bone remodelling that affects perhaps two per cent of Australians over fifty five and is most often found incidentally through an isolated rise in alkaline phosphatase or an abnormal radiograph. The first step in any raised alkaline phosphatase is to establish its source, and a normal gamma glutamyl transferase points away from the liver and towards bone. Common sites are the pelvis, femur, tibia, skull and lumbar spine, and the clinical features follow from expanded, vascular and structurally weak bone: bone pain, warmth over the affected area, deformity such as tibial bowing, deafness from skull involvement, and pathological fracture. A radionuclide bone scan is the most sensitive way to map all affected sites while plain films confirm the characteristic appearance of cortical thickening, trabecular coarsening and expansion. Treatment with a single intravenous zoledronic acid infusion normalises turnover in most patients for years and is indicated for symptomatic disease or for disease at sites where complications threaten, such as the skull base, weight bearing bones or adjacent to major joints.
key_points: A normal gamma glutamyl transferase confirms that a raised alkaline phosphatase is of bony origin.
Bone pain, warmth, deformity and deafness are the characteristic clinical features.
A radionuclide bone scan maps all affected sites and plain films confirm the appearance.
Alkaline phosphatase is normal or low in myeloma, which helps exclude it.
A single zoledronic acid infusion is the usual treatment for symptomatic or high risk disease.
explanation.pearls: A sudden increase in pain or a rapidly enlarging soft tissue mass at a known pagetic site should raise the possibility of osteosarcoma, which complicates well under one per cent of cases but accounts for most Paget related mortality and requires urgent imaging rather than escalation of analgesia.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Investigating raised alkaline phosphatase
BMJ Best Practice: Paget disease of bone

subtopic_detail: Fasting triglycerides above 20 mmol/L found incidentally in a man with poorly controlled diabetes and heavy alcohol use
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 45 year old man in a diabetes clinic. He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin alone and admits he has not been taking it consistently for the past year.

He drinks six standard drinks most evenings. He has no abdominal pain now and has never been admitted with pancreatitis, and he has no personal or family history of cardiovascular disease. The laboratory has telephoned because his fasting lipid sample was grossly lipaemic.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 33 kg/m2, waist circumference 112 cm, eruptive xanthomata over both elbows and the extensor surfaces of the forearms, no hepatomegaly, no abdominal tenderness, no corneal arcus, no tendon xanthomata
data_table.Investigations: Fasting triglycerides 22.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), total cholesterol 9.8 mmol/L (less than 5.5), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.7 mmol/L (greater than 1.0), low density lipoprotein cholesterol not calculable, glycated haemoglobin 10.2 per cent (less than 7.0 for treated diabetes), lipase 38 U/L (less than 60), liver function tests showing an alanine aminotransferase of 68 U/L (less than 40), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management of his lipid abnormality?

options.text: Refer him urgently for therapeutic plasma exchange to clear the circulating triglycerides before starting any oral lipid lowering therapy
options.rationale: Plasma exchange removes triglycerides rapidly but is invasive, resource intensive and reserved for severe hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, particularly with organ failure or in pregnancy. He has no abdominal pain and a normal lipase, so there is no acute indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Commence a high intensity statin as the sole lipid lowering agent and reassess his full lipid profile again in three months
options.rationale: Statins lower triglycerides only modestly and will not bring a level above 20 mmol/L out of the pancreatitis range, although one is eventually indicated for his cardiovascular risk as a man with diabetes. A statin alone is the correct choice once triglycerides are below about 5 mmol/L and low density lipoprotein cholesterol is the target. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Commence ezetimibe and review whether his total cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations have fallen when he returns in three months
options.rationale: Ezetimibe blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption and has almost no effect on triglycerides, so it does not address the abnormality that threatens his pancreas. It is used as an add on to a statin when low density lipoprotein cholesterol targets are not met. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Commence a high dose omega 3 fatty acid preparation as the only agent and review his triglyceride level again in three months
options.rationale: Omega 3 preparations lower triglycerides usefully but less reliably than a fibrate at this magnitude of elevation, and using one alone in a man at immediate risk of pancreatitis is insufficient. They are a reasonable adjunct where a fibrate is not tolerated or the response is incomplete. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Commence a fibrate alongside intensified glycaemic control and a structured plan to reduce his alcohol intake substantially
options.rationale: At triglyceride concentrations above about 10 mmol/L the immediate danger is acute pancreatitis rather than atherosclerosis, and a fibrate is the most effective triglyceride lowering agent while uncontrolled diabetes and alcohol are the two drivers that must be corrected simultaneously. Lipid lowering alone will not succeed while the glycated haemoglobin remains above 10 per cent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

explanation.summary: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia in adults is almost always the product of a genetic predisposition unmasked by acquired factors, of which uncontrolled diabetes, alcohol, obesity, hypothyroidism, renal disease, oestrogen therapy, and drugs such as isotretinoin and second generation antipsychotics are the commonest. The clinical priority shifts at around 10 mmol/L, above which the risk of acute pancreatitis rises steeply and becomes the dominant concern, whereas below that level treatment is driven by cardiovascular risk. Eruptive xanthomata, lipaemia retinalis and a grossly lipaemic sample are the physical correlates of very high concentrations, and laboratory interference means the low density lipoprotein cholesterol cannot be calculated. Treatment combines removal of the acquired drivers with a fibrate, supported by dietary fat restriction, and insulin is added in diabetes both to control glycaemia and because it activates lipoprotein lipase directly. Once triglycerides fall below about 5 mmol/L, attention returns to low density lipoprotein cholesterol and a statin for cardiovascular protection.
key_points: Above about 10 mmol/L the dominant risk is acute pancreatitis rather than atherosclerosis.
Uncontrolled diabetes and alcohol are the two commonest acquired drivers in adults.
Fibrates are the most effective triglyceride lowering agents at this magnitude.
Statins and ezetimibe have little effect on very high triglyceride concentrations.
Once triglycerides fall below about 5 mmol/L, cardiovascular risk reduction resumes priority.
explanation.pearls: Serum lipase can be falsely normal in hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis because the lipaemic sample interferes with the assay, so a patient with severe abdominal pain and triglycerides above 10 mmol/L should be treated as having pancreatitis on clinical and imaging grounds regardless of the enzyme result.

subtopic_detail: Bruising and mouth bleeding in a young adult with pancytopenia, a very low reticulocyte count and no organomegaly
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 22 year old university student referred with three weeks of tiredness and easy bruising. She says her gums bleed when she brushes her teeth and that she has bruises on her legs she cannot account for.

She takes no regular medications, has taken no new supplements and has not travelled. She has had no fevers at home and feels well enough to have attended her lectures this week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pallor of the conjunctivae, scattered petechiae over both shins and two large bruises on the thighs, blood crusting at the gingival margins, no lymphadenopathy anywhere, no hepatomegaly and no splenomegaly, no bone tenderness over the sternum
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 76 g/L (115 to 165) with a mean cell volume of 94 fL (80 to 100), white cell count 1.9 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with a neutrophil count of 0.6 x10^9/L (2.0 to 7.5), platelets 11 x10^9/L (150 to 400), reticulocyte count 6 x10^9/L (20 to 100), blood film showing no blasts and no dysplastic forms, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for presumed immune destruction of the blood cells and review her counts in the clinic in one week
options.rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia affects platelets alone and would not explain the anaemia, neutropenia and profoundly suppressed reticulocyte count, and starting steroids before a marrow diagnosis can obscure the histology. Steroids are appropriate once an immune mechanism has been established. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells and platelets and arrange outpatient haematology review with repeat blood counts in two weeks
options.rationale: Transfusing without a diagnosis and sending her home leaves a profoundly neutropenic young woman exposed to overwhelming infection and delays a diagnosis that determines urgent treatment. Transfusion support is given alongside, not instead of, same day specialist assessment. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

options.text: Start oral iron and a multivitamin preparation and repeat her full blood count and iron studies again in four weeks
options.rationale: Nutritional deficiency does not cause a pancytopenia with this degree of reticulocytopenia, and her mean cell volume, vitamin B12 and folate are all normal. Haematinic replacement is the right answer when a single deficient nutrient is demonstrated. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

options.text: Arrange same day haematology assessment for bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics, alongside transfusion and neutropenic precautions
options.rationale: Pancytopenia with a reticulocyte count this low indicates failure of marrow production rather than peripheral destruction, and only a marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetic studies will separate aplastic anaemia from hypoplastic myelodysplasia or an infiltrative process. The severity of the neutropenia makes this a same day rather than an outpatient problem. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

options.text: Request a computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to search for an occult malignancy causing her blood count abnormalities
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging cannot diagnose a disorder of marrow production and delays the test that will, particularly with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly to pursue. Staging imaging follows a tissue diagnosis when lymphoma or another malignancy is confirmed. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia

explanation.summary: Pancytopenia is approached by asking whether the marrow is failing to produce cells or the periphery is destroying them, and the reticulocyte count is the single most informative discriminator, since a marrow responding appropriately to anaemia raises it. A very low reticulocyte count alongside an absence of organomegaly, lymphadenopathy and circulating blasts points towards acquired aplastic anaemia, an immune mediated destruction of haematopoietic stem cells that peaks in young adults and again in later life. The diagnosis requires a bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing a hypocellular marrow without fibrosis or infiltration, with cytogenetics and flow cytometry to exclude hypoplastic myelodysplastic syndrome and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Severity is graded on the neutrophil, platelet and reticulocyte counts, and severe disease is a medical emergency because untreated it carries very high mortality from infection and bleeding. Treatment is either allogeneic stem cell transplantation, favoured in younger patients with a matched sibling donor, or immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin and ciclosporin, increasingly with eltrombopag added.
key_points: The reticulocyte count separates failure of production from peripheral destruction.
Absent organomegaly, lymphadenopathy and blasts point away from leukaemia and lymphoma.
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics is required to make the diagnosis.
Severe aplastic anaemia is a medical emergency because of infection and bleeding risk.
Treatment is stem cell transplantation or immunosuppression depending on age and donor availability.
explanation.pearls: Avoid transfusing blood products donated by family members in any young person with suspected marrow failure, because alloimmunisation to related donor antigens measurably worsens the outcome of a subsequent allogeneic stem cell transplant from that same family.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aplastic anaemia
National Blood Authority Australia: Patient blood management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Four months of dry tickly cough in a man with a clear chest and normal spirometry who began a blood pressure tablet last year
stem:
You are the general medical registrar seeing a 58 year old man referred with four months of a dry tickly cough that he describes as a constant need to clear his throat. It troubles him most when he lies down and when he talks on the telephone at work.

He produces no sputum, has never wheezed and has no heartburn or acid taste. He has smoked five cigarettes a day for thirty years and has not lost weight. His blood pressure medication was changed eleven months ago and he had no cough before that.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation with no wheeze or crackles, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, oropharynx normal with no cobblestoning or postnasal discharge, no ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph reported as normal with clear lung fields, spirometry showing a forced expiratory volume in one second of 92 per cent predicted with a ratio of 0.78 and no bronchodilator response, full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor twice daily for eight weeks and review whether his cough has settled at the end of the course
options.rationale: Reflux related cough is a genuine cause and can occur without heartburn, but it should not be pursued ahead of a drug cause that has a clear temporal relationship and is reversible within weeks. Acid suppression is the next step once the medication has been changed and the cough persists. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest to exclude a malignancy given his smoking history and the duration of the cough
options.rationale: Chronic cough in a smoker always deserves a thought about malignancy, but he has a normal chest radiograph, no haemoptysis, no weight loss and no clubbing or lymphadenopathy, and a reversible drug cause that is easily tested. Computed tomography is warranted if the cough persists after the drug is withdrawn or if any red flag emerges. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory

options.text: Commence a trial of inhaled corticosteroid for eight weeks on the basis that cough variant asthma is the likeliest explanation
options.rationale: Cough variant asthma produces a nocturnal or exercise related cough with variable airflow obstruction or bronchodilator responsiveness, and his spirometry is normal with no response. An inhaled corticosteroid trial, ideally with sputum eosinophil counts, belongs later in the pathway. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Substitute his angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker and reassess his cough after four weeks
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor cough affects up to one in ten users, is characteristically dry and tickly, and can begin anywhere from hours to a year after the drug is started, which makes the delayed onset here entirely consistent. Angiotensin receptor blockers do not cause the cough because they do not inhibit bradykinin breakdown, so substitution both tests and treats the hypothesis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Prescribe an intranasal corticosteroid with an oral antihistamine for upper airway cough syndrome and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Upper airway cough syndrome is a leading cause of chronic cough but is suggested by postnasal discharge, throat cobblestoning or nasal symptoms, none of which he has. It is the reasonable next trial once a drug cause has been excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory

explanation.summary: Chronic cough is defined as a cough lasting more than eight weeks and, in a non smoker with a normal chest radiograph, is dominated by three causes: upper airway cough syndrome, asthma or eosinophilic bronchitis, and gastro oesophageal reflux. Before working through that triad, the single most rewarding step is to review the medication list, because angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are among the most widely prescribed drugs in Australia and cause cough in up to a tenth of those taking them. The mechanism is accumulation of bradykinin and substance P in the airway rather than any structural change, which explains why the cough is dry and tickly, why examination and investigations are normal, and why angiotensin receptor blockers are a safe substitute. The characteristic that trips clinicians up is the timing, since onset ranges from the first dose to a year of uneventful use, so a long period of tolerance does not exclude the drug. Resolution usually begins within one to four weeks of withdrawal but occasionally takes up to three months, so the trial must be given adequate time before the cause is dismissed.
key_points: Review the medication list before working through the chronic cough triad.
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor cough affects up to ten per cent of users.
Onset ranges from hours to a year after starting, so delayed onset does not exclude the drug.
Angiotensin receptor blockers do not cause cough and are a direct substitute.
Resolution usually occurs within one to four weeks but can take up to three months.
explanation.pearls: Allow up to three months after withdrawal before concluding that an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor was not the cause of a chronic cough, because a minority of patients take that long to settle and rechallenging or investigating too early sends them down an unnecessary diagnostic pathway.

subtopic_detail: Severe wet season pneumonia in a Top End man with diabetes and heavy alcohol use growing a Gram negative bacillus
stem:
You are the general medical registrar in a Darwin hospital in February admitting a 52 year old man with five days of fever, productive cough and increasing breathlessness. He works maintaining irrigation lines on a market garden and has been out in heavy rain and mud most of the week.

He has type 2 diabetes with a glycated haemoglobin of 11.4 per cent and drinks heavily. He was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin in the emergency department twelve hours ago and has deteriorated since, now requiring 8 litres per minute of oxygen. The laboratory has telephoned to say both blood culture bottles are growing a Gram negative bacillus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 91 per cent on 8 litres per minute of oxygen, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bronchial breathing at the right upper zone with coarse crackles bilaterally, no skin abscess or ulcer found on full skin survey, no neck stiffness, no joint effusion, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph showing right upper lobe consolidation with a developing cavity, white cell count 18.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein 342 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60 to 110), lactate 3.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0), glycated haemoglobin 11.4 per cent (less than 7.0 for treated diabetes), blood cultures growing a Gram negative bacillus with bipolar staining

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Continue ceftriaxone and add oral doxycycline to cover atypical and zoonotic causes of community acquired pneumonia in this region
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is unreliable against the organism suggested here and doxycycline has no role in the intensive phase of treatment, so this leaves a rapidly progressive infection inadequately covered. Doxycycline is relevant to other tropical zoonoses such as Q fever, leptospirosis and rickettsial infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Change to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate once he is afebrile and continue it for a total course of three weeks after discharge
options.rationale: Oral therapy has no place in the intensive phase of a severe cavitating pneumonia with bacteraemia and shock, and amoxicillin with clavulanate is inferior for this organism. It is sometimes used as a second line eradication agent in pregnancy or intolerance, after the intravenous phase is complete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Change to intravenous gentamicin combined with amoxicillin to broaden Gram negative cover while awaiting formal identification and sensitivities
options.rationale: Aminoglycosides and amoxicillin are both ineffective against this organism, which is intrinsically resistant to gentamicin, and this combination would be actively harmful in a man with acute kidney injury. Gentamicin remains useful for other Gram negative sepsis where renal function permits. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Change to intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam as broad spectrum cover for a Gram negative bacteraemia with a pulmonary source
options.rationale: Piperacillin with tazobactam covers most Gram negative organisms but is not recommended for this infection, where carbapenem or ceftazidime therapy is supported by mortality data from Australian trials. It is a reasonable empirical choice for healthcare associated Gram negative sepsis without this epidemiological picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Change to intravenous meropenem and plan a prolonged intensive phase followed by months of oral eradication therapy
options.rationale: Wet season cavitating pneumonia with septic shock in a Top End man with diabetes and soil exposure, growing a bipolar staining Gram negative bacillus, is melioidosis, and Burkholderia pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to the usual community acquired pneumonia regimens. Treatment requires an intensive phase of at least two weeks with meropenem or ceftazidime followed by at least three months of oral eradication therapy to prevent relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, an environmental saprophyte of soil and surface water across northern Australia and South East Asia, and cases cluster sharply in the monsoonal wet season when the organism is brought to the surface and aerosolised. Diabetes is the single strongest risk factor, followed by hazardous alcohol use, chronic lung disease, chronic kidney disease and immunosuppression, and around four fifths of patients have at least one. Pneumonia is the commonest presentation and may cavitate and progress rapidly to septic shock, while other presentations include skin abscesses, genitourinary infection, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, parotid abscess in children and central nervous system disease. The organism is intrinsically resistant to penicillins, gentamicin and most cephalosporins other than ceftazidime, which is why standard community acquired pneumonia regimens fail. Treatment has two phases: an intensive intravenous phase of at least two weeks with meropenem or ceftazidime, extended for deep seated infection, followed by at least three months of oral eradication therapy with trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, and relapse follows incomplete eradication.
key_points: Wet season presentation with soil or water exposure in northern Australia is the epidemiological signature.
Diabetes and hazardous alcohol use are the dominant host risk factors.
The organism is intrinsically resistant to penicillins, gentamicin and most cephalosporins.
Intensive phase is at least two weeks of meropenem or ceftazidime intravenously.
Eradication requires at least three months of oral therapy to prevent relapse.
explanation.pearls: Extend the intravenous intensive phase to four weeks for deep seated disease and to eight weeks for central nervous system, bone or joint involvement, because relapse rates rise sharply when a fourteen day course is applied to infection at these sites.
